meta.name: Sigil Core — Network / Exfiltration
meta.author: NOMARJ <hello@sigilsec.ai>
meta.description: Detects outbound network activity, webhook calls, raw sockets, DNS exfiltration, and data upload patterns

rules.remediation: Confirm the destination is one the package documents. Outbound HTTP is normal in clients and abnormal in a formatter; the domain decides.
Confirm the destination is documented and expected for this package.
Confirm the destination is documented and expected for this package.
Confirm the fetched URL is documented and owned by the package's maintainers.
Confirm the destination is documented and expected for this package.

rules.description: Webhook or callback URL assigned to an external endpoint
rules.remediation: Check what the webhook receives. A webhook that posts scan output, environment details or file contents is exfiltration.
Remove the endpoint. These services exist to receive out-of-band callbacks and file drops; there is no legitimate reason for shipped code to talk to one.
Raw sockets in agent tooling need a documented reason (a custom protocol, a health check). Without one, treat as a reverse-shell precursor.
Verify the address. A connect() to a hard-coded host and port is the reverse-shell shape.
DNS resolution is benign on its own; check that no encoded data is placed in the hostname.
Data is base64-encoded right where it is read — the standard step before exfiltration. Trace where the encoded value goes.

A curl/wget with a URL is how skills document an API and how installers fetch releases, so on its own it is an observation (Low) and never moves the verdict. Confirm the host is the one the skill documents and pin what is fetched. Piping the download straight into an interpreter is reported separately as NET-RCE-001.

rules.description: Remote script piped straight into an interpreter (download-and-execute)
rules.remediation: The command downloads code and runs it in one step, so what executes is whatever the server returns at that moment, never anything a reviewer saw. Check the host: a vendor's documented installer is a known (still unreviewed) shape and the best-known ones are allow-listed; an unknown domain, a URL shortener, a raw IP, a paste site or an attacker-controlled GitHub path is the dropper shape. Prefer a pinned release with a checksum, or a package manager.

rules.description: Windows executable or script downloaded with curl.exe, wget, Invoke-WebRequest, BITS or certutil
rules.remediation: A command line fetches a Windows program or script (.exe, .msi, .scr, .ps1, .bat, .vbs, .hta, .dll) from a URL. An installer that documents its own download from the vendor's release page is ordinary; a package that builds this command in code — in the measured samples a `curl.exe -L <raw GitHub URL>/x.exe -o <cwd>\x.exe` string passed to `powershell -Command`, followed by `Start-Process` on the same path — is a dropper. Medium on its own; DROPPER-CHAIN-001 reports it at High when the downloaded path is then launched. Check the URL's owner and what runs the file.

rules.description: curl uploads a local file (-F name=@file, --data-binary @file, -T file)
rules.remediation: An observation, not a finding on its own: uploading a build artifact or a report is what deploy and CI scripts do. Read which file is sent and to whom. It matters when the file is something the user did not choose to publish — a credential file, the host's configuration, or a project archive that still carries .env (AGENTSC-CHAIN-002 and EXFIL-CHAIN-001 report those links at High and Critical).

rules.description: URL whose host is a public IPv4 address
rules.remediation: The code talks to a bare public IP address instead of a named host. Services a package legitimately depends on have names (and TLS certificates for them); a hard-coded address is how beacons, droppers and dependency-confusion callbacks reach a server that has no domain to seize. Loopback, private, link-local and documentation ranges and the public DNS resolvers are not reported. Find out who owns the address and what is sent to it; INSTALL-RAWIP-001 reports the same URL at High when it sits in setup.py, a package __init__.py or package.json, where it runs or resolves at install or import time.

Choosing a transport is expected in any MCP server or client, so on its own this is informational: stdio keeps the tool channel on the local machine, while SSE or Streamable HTTP puts it on the network. For a network transport, check which host the client connects to or the server listens on: a documented endpoint or localhost is normal; a client pointed at an unfamiliar remote URL sends every tool call and result (including any file contents or secrets in the arguments) off the machine, and a server bound to 0.0.0.0 without authentication lets anyone who can reach the port invoke its tools.

An MCP proxy sits between the agent and its tool servers and sees, and can rewrite, every tool description, call and result that passes through it. A proxy the operator chose and documented (a stdio-to-HTTP bridge such as mcp-proxy or mcp-remote pointed at a known server, or an enterprise MCP gateway) is normal; one introduced by a package or dependency, or one forwarding to a host you do not recognise, is interception of the whole tool channel, so remove it or verify the upstream URL before approving.

rules.description: Cloud instance-metadata (IMDS) endpoint — SSRF / credential theft
rules.remediation: A package should never query the instance-metadata service: that is where cloud credentials are harvested from. Remove the request, or if this is deliberate cloud bootstrap code, mark the line with sigil-reviewed-imds.

rules.description: Dynamic-DNS or developer-tunnel host — C2 shape
rules.remediation: Shipped code pointing at a tunnel or dynamic-DNS host is the command-and-control shape. Replace with a fixed, owned domain, or remove it.

rules.description: URL on a TLD frequently abused for malware and phishing
rules.remediation: Verify who owns the domain. This is a weak signal on its own; it matters when it appears next to a download, a credential read or an obfuscated payload.

rules.description: Cryptominer indicator — mining pool URL or miner binary
rules.remediation: Do not install. A stratum pool URL or a miner binary inside agent tooling has no benign reading; the package mines with your CPU.

rules.description: DNS lookup of encoded data — DNS exfiltration
rules.remediation: Encoding data into a hostname and resolving it is exfiltration that bypasses HTTP egress controls. Remove it.

rules.description: API base URL hardcoded to a plaintext-HTTP remote host
rules.remediation: A base URL or endpoint constant names a remote host over plain http://. Every request the client makes — the API key in its auth header, the prompt, the response — crosses the network unencrypted to that host, and a hardcoded host that is not the provider the package claims to use is a proxy that sees all of it. Local, private-network and documentation hosts are not reported. Use the provider's https endpoint, or take the URL from configuration, and reject a package that routes your key through an undocumented relay.

A script is fetched from a link-shortening service (is.gd, bit.ly, tinyurl, …) and piped straight into a shell or PowerShell's Invoke-Expression. The shortener hides where the script comes from and can be re-pointed at any time, so what runs tomorrow is not what a reviewer saw today; no legitimate installer needs one. Do not run the line; resolve the link without executing it and report the package.

correlation_rules.description: Credential read reaches a network send (exfiltration chain)
correlation_rules.remediation: A secret read from the environment or a credential file is sent in the body of an outbound request. That is credential exfiltration; do not install, and report the package.

A download writes a file (`open(PATH, 'wb')` under the response, `curl -o "$OUT"`, `curl.exe ... -o "{output_file}"`, `urlretrieve(url, path)`) and a few lines later the same path is launched: `subprocess.run(["python3", PATH])`, `Start-Process "{output_file}"`, `os.startfile(path)`. That is download-and-execute split across lines — the NET-RCE-001 shape without the pipe — and in the measured samples it ran at import time from a package's __init__.py (a .pyz from a look-alike domain) and from three PyPI droppers fetching an .exe. Nothing the package ships tells a reviewer what the downloaded program does. Pin the artifact by hash and verify it before running it, or reject the package.
